transcript.text: quick q: churn with 3% positives, should i report PR-AUC or ROC-AUC to my manager, and why? no data work, just the answer

I've started a sourced answer for you. Here's the short version.

**Report PR-AUC as your headline number, and mention ROC-AUC only as a secondary figure.**

**Why**
- **ROC-AUC can look good when the model is mediocre.** It includes the false positive rate, and that rate divides by the huge pool of non-churners (about 97%). Hundreds of false alarms barely change that rate, so ROC-AUC can stay around 0.85–0.90 even when most of your flagged customers aren't churners.
- **PR-AUC shows what your manager cares about.** Precision is "of the customers we flag, how many really churn?" Recall is "of the people who really churn, how many do we catch?" Those two numbers decide how much a retention campaign costs and how much it saves.
- **PR-AUC needs a baseline to read.** A random model scores about 0.03 on PR-AUC, which is the positive rate. A PR-AUC of 0.25 is therefore roughly 8 times better than random. Without that baseline the number looks small to someone who expects values near 1.

**How to present it**
- Give PR-AUC next to the 3% baseline, for example "0.25 vs 0.03 for random".
- Add one concrete operating point, for example "If we contact the top 5% of customers by risk, about X% of them will churn, and we'll reach about Y% of all churners." This is easier for a manager to act on than any single AUC.
- Mention ROC-AUC only if someone asks for it or you need to compare with older reports. Say that it tends to look flattering on imbalanced data.

**Caveat:** ROC-AUC isn't wrong. It measures how well the model ranks a random churner above a random non-churner, and it doesn't depend on the class balance. If the business question is only about ranking quality, it's fine. For a campaign with a limited budget, PR-AUC fits better.
